BHARAT AI-SoC CHALLENGE 2026–27 · PROBLEM STATEMENT 3 · TEAM ENTITY · V S KAMALESH · VERSION 0.5.3

ENTITY Shield

On-device threat, phishing and scam detection on an Arm phone. Detectors decide in milliseconds; Llama 3.2 on ExecuTorch explains in English or Hindi. Nothing leaves the phone.
1.000 / 0.915SMS "scam" precision / recall, unseen Indian templates (app verdict)

1. Problem and approach

Scam SMS (fake KYC, electricity cut-offs, courier "customs", "digital arrest", UPI refund tricks, part-time job scams) reach every Indian phone, and the people most at risk are the least able to spot them. Cloud scanners need the message to leave the phone. ENTITY Shield does all of it on the phone's Arm CPU:

  • Two-tier design. Small ExecuTorch detectors (130 KB each) score every SMS, link and network event in milliseconds and decide the verdict. Llama 3.2 1B on ExecuTorch only explains a flagged item, in plain English or Hindi.
  • Llama can't overrule or invent. The verdict and the remediation steps are not generated. The app writes the start of Llama's answer (verdict prefill) and gives it a short fact sheet, so it explains why.
  • Phone-only network protection. A local DNS-only VPN sees every app's lookups (attributed per app) and a LAN tripwire catches devices probing the phone. That covers the network-intrusion and malware-behaviour parts of PS3 with no extra hardware.

2. Architecture

Inputs: SMS_RECEIVED, inbox, share/select-text/Link Guard, the DNS VPN and the tripwire → detectors (SMS, URL, behaviour rules) → verdict (safe / suspicious / dangerous) → instant notification with fixed steps → when the user opens the alert, Llama streams the explanation. Coexistence rules:

  • Detection never waits for Llama.
  • Llama loads on demand and frees its ~1.3 GB after 90 s.
  • Llama runs only while an alert is on screen.
  • The fixed system prompt is pre-filled into the KV cache when an alert fires (ExecuTorch prefillPrompt).

Latency budget. The warning is instant; the explanation follows on the user's screen. The grey bar is the mistake we measured and removed (§7).

3. Detectors

Features: hashed character 2–5-grams (32,768 slots, FNV-1a) plus 15 named signals for SMS and 11 for URL. The signals include urgency, OTP/PIN requests, payment requests, threats, prize and job lures, authority claims, KYC/Aadhaar, brand-vs-domain mismatch, shorteners, and sender is a 10-digit mobile number vs a registered DLT header such as VM-HDFCBK. Model: logistic regression, exported as one Linear + sigmoid ExecuTorch program (XNNPACK). Data: UCI SMS Spam Collection (only spam with a fraud cue counts as scam: Shield detects fraud, not marketing), plus 143 hand-written Indian templates (47 scam families, 96 legitimate: bank OTP and debit alerts, UPI, deliveries, bills, missed-call and data alerts, DLT promotions, government advisories, personal Hinglish/Hindi). For URLs: PhishTank (time split), OpenPhish, Tranco. The test sets hold out whole templates and the newest phishing.

Same answer on the phone. The app's Kotlin featurizer is a line-by-line port of the Python one. The golden vectors pass in Python, on the JVM (unit tests) and on the phone through the production path: SMS 43/43, URL 40/40, max difference 6×10⁻⁷. Retraining on Windows reproduced the Mac model bit-exactly (max difference 0.0).

Faster by measuring. 98% of detection time was featurizing: a String per n-gram, plus a fresh 131 KB dense vector copied into a tensor on every call. An allocation-free featurizer and one reused direct FloatBuffer per ExecuTorch model (Tensor.fromBlob) took the full SMS check from 9.4 ms to 5.0 ms p50 and the URL check from 2.7 to 1.1 ms on the Dimensity 7300, with parity unchanged. Built the way it ships (R8), the same checks take 0.64 ms (SMS) and 0.15 ms (URL) on the Dimensity 7300 and 0.50 / 0.11 ms on the Snapdragon 7s Gen 3.

URL v3. The first URL model learned benign data from bare domains only (flipkart.com). DNS lookups are full hostnames (connekt.flipkart.net), so it called many of them phishing. v3 adds real DNS hostnames from the Cisco Umbrella list, split by registrable domain so no domain is on both sides, and a brand_lure signal for brand names inside unrelated domains. On 20,000 held-out real hostnames it raises 1.06% false alarms at the link threshold and 0.1% at Network Guard's blocking threshold.

3b. The scam gate, and what the whole app gets right

On a real 4,620-message inbox the 0.5.0 model called 537 messages a scam and 1573 suspicious: Jio data and missed-call alerts, bank login alerts, TRAI and DoT advisories, promotions. It had learned "marketing" as well as "fraud". 0.5.1 adds a rule layer after the models (ScamGate.kt, the same rules as sms_gate in Python; a unit test checks both agree on 2,871 cases). A message is called a scam only with a fraud-specific cue: it asks you to hand over a code or PIN, ties a threat to a link or a personal number to call, has a brand look-alike link, is a task-job lure, or carries a link the URL model calls phishing. Without one, a registered business sender is safe ("promotion, not a scam" when it reads like one), a delivered login code is safe, and anything else is at most "be careful". A message from a saved contact is never called a scam (at most "be careful" when it carries a fraud cue, in case the contact was hacked), and the user's own "scam / not a scam" answers apply to similar messages from then on.

Trade-off and honest reading.
  • On unseen Indian templates the gate raises the precision of a "scam" call from 0.848 to 1.000 and cuts false alarms from 6.00% to 0.00%. With "be careful" counted it flags 93.25% of scams.
  • The price is paid on UCI (UK spam, 2011): only 76.67% of its fraud gets flagged, against 90.00% for the model alone. Its lures (premium-rate call-backs, "you have won" without a link) lack the Indian fraud cues the gate looks for. Fewer false alarms cost missed scams; the gate makes that trade on purpose for Indian users.
  • 0.5.3, scam gate v5, built on the validation split only (scripts/analyze_sms_misses.py): Hindi "{number} पर कॉल करें" call-backs and service-cut threats, "send the code you received", premium-rate prizes, police words only with something to do, payment receipts, government links and the sending brand's own deep links. On validation, Indian scams went from 80 missed to 0. The test split above was run once, after the rules were final. Held-out scams still missed (34 of 400): spoofed bank-header frauds, tax refund, courier, loan and investment templates.
  • Where the rules were tuned. The gate was written against a 64-message challenge set and the inbox above, so these are not held-out numbers: on the inbox, 0.5.1 gives 6 scam and 46 suspicious of 4,620; on the phone, 11 of the newest 1,000 were flagged, 2 of them real scams, and none was missed in a 40-message sample of the rest. On 23 Nov 0.5.3 flagged 7 of the newest 1,000, all of them scams by the owner's saved answers (a personalised result: those answers are applied by the app itself). The untouched checks are the held-out split above and 19 messages written after tuning: 0 of 15 legitimate ones called scam, 4 of 4 scams called scam.

4. Network Guard: network intrusion and malware behaviour, on the phone

  • DNS-only local VPN. Only the fake resolver address is routed into the TUN interface, so app traffic never flows through Shield. Each question is parsed (IPv4/UDP/DNS, unit-tested) and attributed to its app with getConnectionOwnerUid. It is scored on the phone (allow-lists, then the URL model), then either forwarded to the network's own resolver or answered NXDOMAIN if dangerous.
  • Lookup policy v2 (DnsPolicy). v1 blocked whenever the URL model said "scam" and stopped ordinary traffic: on the Infinix, the phone maker's Messages servers, Airtel's backend and an Indian SMS-link service. v2 lets through local names, OS/CDN infrastructure, sites the user allowed, Tranco top-1M domains and the asking app's own domains; blocks hosts on the bundled PhishTank/OpenPhish list; blocks on the model only above a 0.1%-false-alarm threshold; and only flags the rest.
    Blocked by mistake / phishing caughtv1v2
    Long-tail legitimate domains with real subdomain prefixes (20,000)21.5%0.03%
    Held-out real DNS hostnames, Umbrella ranks 600k–1M (20,000)10.5%0.12%
    PhishTank time-split (3,393), model alone65%33% (the feed list adds the known ones)
    OpenPhish held-out (297), model alone93%87%
  • Malware behaviour (per app):
    • Beacon: 6 or more lookups of one domain at a near-constant interval.
    • DGA burst: 8 or more different non-existent names within 60 s.
    • DNS tunnel: 15 or more unique subdomains, or long high-entropy labels.
    Each becomes an alert naming the app, with "remove app" as the action.
  • LAN tripwire. Decoy listeners on 2222, 2323, 5555, 8080, 8443 and 9999. Any contact means another device on the Wi-Fi is probing the phone: a scan (3 or more ports within 30 s), password guessing (5 or more connections to one port), or an ADB-worm probe (port 5555).
  • Test app. beaconsim imitates a C2 beacon, a DGA burst and DNS exfiltration using only DNS lookups of made-up names, so the alerts name a real installed app.

5. Link sandbox: follow the link instead of guessing

The phone visits the link itself over raw HTTP/1.1: no cookies, no JavaScript, private addresses refused, redirects followed one by one, the certificate captured, size and time capped. The page is parsed inside an Android isolatedProcess service that has no access to Shield's files and no network; both are checked on every end-to-end run. The report shows where the link really lands, the certificate, and what the page asks for (UPI PIN, ATM PIN, OTP, Aadhaar, PAN, card and CVV). Strong signals: secret fields, forms or scripts that send data to Telegram or Discord bots, brand copies, look-alike domains, APK downloads. Weak signals (common on honest Indian sites) only nudge.

Honest reading. On the held-out sample the sandbox did not catch more phishing than the address model. Its value is what the address cannot show. The held-out sample also found a cloaking kit that sent the sandbox on to the real roblox.com; since 0.4.0 a risky address that lands on a trusted site stays flagged. A page that is gone or never answers is reported as "Couldn't check this link", never as safe.

6. Llama 3.2 1B on ExecuTorch: the explanation layer

Model: Meta's quantization-aware-trained Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-QLORA_INT4_EO8, exported with ExecuTorch 1.5.1 (XNNPACK, 4-bit groupwise weights, 8-bit dynamic activations, KV cache, custom SDPA, context 2048; 1.12 GB). It runs in the APK through LlmModule (the official ExecuTorch 1.5.1 Android library). The app downloads this exact file from Meta/PyTorch's Hugging Face repository (executorch-community), SHA-256 checked, with the project's GitHub release as fallback; the tokenizer ships in the APK. While an answer is being written, a short foreground service keeps the phone's app freezer from pausing it. It was chosen over our own 8da4w export (faster) because it never refused and wrote fluent Hindi in our October tests. Prompt: fact sheet (KYC = Know Your Customer; banks never ask for OTP/PIN by SMS link; a UPI PIN only sends money; police never arrest over video calls; helpline 1930) + the detector's evidence + verdict prefill. Without the prefill the 1B refused to explain scams at all.

Quality: 40 held-out scam messages, English and Hindi, on the phone

Honest reading. The automatic checks (refusal, invented links or numbers, contradiction) almost always pass, but a manual read found real errors. In English, 4 of the 40 answers invent a "PIN/password" detail on UK premium-rate spam; none were wrong on the Indian messages. In Hindi, 2 answers negated the evidence (e.g. "did not come from a personal number"). This is why Llama never decides and never writes the steps, and it is the main Phase 2 target (distillation + LoRA on the QAT checkpoint). Manual labels: benchmarks/results/llm_explain_manual_review_*.json, reviewed with AI assistance and pending a native-speaker check.

Pre-warming the system prompt

When an alert fires, the fixed 99-token system prompt is pre-filled into the KV cache (LlmModule.prefillPrompt), so opening the alert costs only the message's own 134 tokens. In the app on the Infinix (foreground, same alert, greedy), the first token arrives after 1.00 s pre-warmed vs 1.78 s cold (−44%). The pre-warmed answer matches the cold one for its first 14 tokens, then picks an equally correct wording. This is consistent with a near-tie flipping under a different floating-point summation order when the prompt is prefilled in two chunks; we have not confirmed it directly. Removing the literal BOS token from the prefilled text diverged from the first sentence, so prefillPrompt adds no BOS of its own.

7. Arm SoC: where the time goes

Measured with ExecuTorch's own llama_main under taskset. The only things that change are the thread count and the allowed cores. Masks come from each phone's cpuinfo_max_freq; arms are interleaved over 3 runs.

PhoneArmThreadsMaskPrefill tok/sDecode tok/sTTFT (165 tok)
Infinix X6878t4_big4f0185.6 ± 0.619.20.89 s
Infinix X6878default-1all171.0 ± 4.418.70.96 s
Infinix X6878t44all170.1 ± 6.619.30.97 s
Infinix X6878naive88all162.6 ± 8.115.51.01 s
Infinix X6878t3_big3e0153.8 ± 2.819.01.07 s
Infinix X6878t4_little4f47.5 ± 0.19.63.48 s
Three findings.
  1. Android's background cgroup moves ExecuTorch to the little cores. Our first build ran Llama on a THREAD_PRIORITY_BACKGROUND thread. /proc/<pid>/task/*/cgroup showed every XNNPACK worker in cpuset:/background: prefill 25 tok/s and a 9.2 s first token on the Dimensity 7300. The little-core row above reproduces the effect (3.9× slower prefill). Llama now runs at normal priority, only while its alert is on screen.
  2. ExecuTorch's thread heuristic picks 3 threads on the Dimensity 7300, because midr_el1 is unreadable and it falls back. On the Snapdragon, 3 instead of 4 big-core threads costs 17% of prefill.
  3. ENTITY's llama.cpp result holds on ExecuTorch and on Armv9 (A720/A520, i8mm). 8 threads cost 19% decode. Pinning to the big cores gives the fastest and steadiest prefill (±0.6 vs ±6.6 tok/s).
Inside the app it did not carry over. 0.5.0 shipped an ExecuTorch build patched to pin its 4 threads to the big cores. In the app it measured 7.8–11 tok/s decode, not 19: Android resets a thread's CPU affinity whenever the app moves between cpusets (foreground, top-app, background), so the pinning did not last. 0.5.1 went back to the official library: 15.5 tok/s decode, 1.0 s first token pre-warmed, 1.8 s cold in the app on the Infinix (bench_inapp_Infinix_X6878_2026-11-19.csv). The patch is kept in backup/executorch/.

7b. Sustained load: temperature, memory and speed

30 Llama answers back to back with no pause (4.8 min; Infinix X6878, SM7635, Android 16, on USB power; scripts/bench_sustained.py, the loop run as a script on the phone). Each answer is an alert explanation: a 162-token prompt (verdict, warning signs, the SMS) and up to 160 new tokens. Decode, average of the first three answers vs the last three: 18.61 → 19.09 tok/s; time to first token 1.14 → 1.04 s. Hottest CPU zone 43.3 °C at the start, 61.4 °C at its peak; battery 36.0 → 38.0 °C. Slowest single answer: 16.3 tok/s, so no thermal throttling showed in this run. Peak memory of the runner: 1552 MiB on the first answer, 1552 MiB on the last (no growth). The app at rest with the detectors loaded and no Llama: 163.8 MB PSS. Model files: Llama 1.12 GB, detectors 130 KB each.

8. App: design and smoothness

A new design system (graphite and signal lime, light and dark, Geist type, a custom icon set) with a liquid-glass tab bar rendered by the app itself: the backdrop is recorded into a GraphicsLayer and redrawn through an AGSL lens and a blur. The glass falls back to blur-only on Android 12 and to a frosted tint on Android 10–11, low-RAM phones and Battery Saver. Tabs are built once and kept, so a switch never builds a screen mid-animation. scripts/bench_ui.py taps through the tabs 30 times and reads dumpsys gfxinfo:

PhoneJanky framesp95 framep99 frame
CMF Phone 1 (Dimensity 7300, 120 Hz)4.0% → 1.15%150 → 48 ms1100 → 65 ms
Infinix X6878 (Snapdragon 7s Gen 3, 120 Hz)7.1% → 2.4%53 → 27 ms117 → 30 ms

R8, resource shrinking and a startup profile took the APK from 33 MB to 17 MB. Llama installs from inside the app (resumable download from Hugging Face, GitHub fallback, SHA-256 checked).

10. Privacy, security and limits

No account, analytics or cloud call. Messages, links and lookups are judged on the phone. The INTERNET permission is used to forward the phone's own DNS lookups to its usual resolver, to visit a link in the sandbox when the user asks, and for the optional one-time Llama download. The inbox audit exports counts only. Test hooks exist only in debug and QA builds, behind the DUMP permission. Full table: docs/PRIVACY.md.

  • Data used. Training and test sets are public datasets (UCI, PhishTank, OpenPhish, Tranco, Cisco Umbrella) and message templates written for this project. No real person's messages are in them, so they can be shared in full.
  • The one real inbox is the developer's own phone, checked with his consent: on the phone by the app's Inbox audit (only counts leave) and once on a laptop from a local copy deleted afterwards. Only counts are in the repository.
  • What the app keeps. Alert text is deleted on its own (safe items after 7 days, alerts after 30). The user's "scam / not a scam" answers keep only the message's words with numbers, codes and amounts removed and links cut to their domain. The contacts check asks Android "is this number saved?" and reads nothing else.
  • Always on, with the app closed. Android starts Shield for each SMS; Network Guard restarts after a reboot or update if it was on; the app walks the user through battery, auto-start and Always-on VPN settings. "Force stop" switches it off until the app is opened again.
  • Network Guard sees this phone's own traffic, not other devices. Strict Private DNS or in-app DNS-over-HTTPS bypasses its DNS view.
  • Test data: the Indian SMS test set is templated, and the real-inbox numbers come from one phone whose false alarms were used to write the scam gate. A labelled set from other consented phones is the first Phase 2 task.
  • URL recall from the address alone is 0.53 on the PhishTank time split and 0.92 on OpenPhish: hostname only, by design. The sandbox reads HTML without running JavaScript.
  • Llama 1B is wrong 10–15% of the time on hard inputs, so it explains but never decides.

11. Phase 2 plan

  • Network:
    • A full-tunnel flow meter with NetFlow features.
    • A flow intrusion model on NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 / NF-CSE-CIC-IDS2018-v2, with a cross-dataset test.
    • A per-app anomaly baseline (ExecuTorch on-device training, TrainingModule).
  • Llama: distilled English/Hindi explanation data and LoRA on the QAT checkpoint (as "Llama-…" per the licence); prefix-KV reuse; Tamil.
  • Evaluation: a consented, anonymised SMS set from 10–20 phones never used for tuning; signed, verified updates of the phishing feed and detector weights.
  • Coverage: WhatsApp/Telegram notifications, call screening ("digital arrest"), UPI QR checks, a field trial with 10–20 phones.
  • Arm: the KleidiAI on/off ablation (custom AAR), a Mali GPU (Vulkan) delegate for the detectors, and upstreaming the ExecuTorch Windows flatc lookup fix and the core-count heuristic fix.
